archetype.name: Dual-Threat (scramble-first)
archetype.definition: An undersized, undrafted rookie whose real production comes when the pocket breaks and he runs, not from designed runs or from attacking the middle of the field through the air.

report.headline: Legs kept Tampa afloat for three starts; the passing never did
report.take:
Jalon Daniels was a three-week bridge. He started Weeks 4 through 6 while Baker Mayfield was out, went 1-2, and has been back at QB2 since Mayfield returned in Week 7. His only snaps since were a 10% cameo in the Week 7 rout of Carolina. In those three starts he averaged 31.7 attempts, 167 passing yards and 39 rushing yards. The shape of his game is clear even from a small sample: a scramble-first improviser playing in an offense built to hide its quarterback. Tampa's pass rate over expected (-7.5) ranks 30th, and its defense ranks 3rd by EPA.

The legs are the real part. He scrambled on 13% of his dropbacks, those scrambles averaged 0.377 EPA, and 7 of the 16 moved the chains. His 24.6 rushing yards a game rank 11th among 55 qualifiers. He was called for only two designed runs, so this is improvisation, not scheme. The arm is the problem. He threw at an average depth of 5.23 intended air yards, 4.15 yards short of the sticks, and his 5.11 yards per attempt ranks 50th. His 18.4% bad-throw rate ranks 42nd of 45. The intermediate window is where it fell apart: 19 throws between 10 and 19 air yards, 26.3% completed, a CPOE of -29 and two interceptions.

The numbers hide where the damage happened. Most of his negative passing EPA came in one-score games (-0.229 a play, all five of his interceptions), and close fourth quarters were the worst of it: 24 plays at -0.522 EPA with three picks. The Pittsburgh start alone (22/43, -18.7 EPA, five sacks, two picks) is close to his whole season total. He was pressured on only 19.2% of dropbacks that day, so it wasn't the line; his bad-throw rate hit 26.8%. Some things flatter him. His only clean passing day came against Dallas, now the 32nd-ranked defense. The 0.7 EPA on deep balls is nine attempts, and three red-zone touchdowns on nine plays won't hold. Some things cut against him: his top target Emeka Egbuka drew 29 targets at -0.447 EPA apiece, a connection that never worked.

Going forward he is insurance, not a starter. If Mayfield goes down again, expect the same profile: useful rushing, short passing, turnovers when he has to throw to keep up. In a run-first, defense-led team that is survivable for a game or two, not a path to winning.

strengths.title: Scrambles that actually pay
strengths.body: He breaks the pocket often, on 13% of dropbacks, and when he does the play gains value: 0.377 EPA per scramble and seven first downs on 16 runs. This is his best skill and the most stable part of his game, because it's athletic instinct rather than a hot split. It also partly offsets a 33.3% pressure-to-sack rate, the cost of holding the ball looking to escape.

strengths.title: Efficient near the goal line
strengths.body: Nine red-zone plays produced three touchdowns, 0.392 EPA a play and a +13.1 CPOE, where the field compresses and short throws are enough. It's a real sign he can finish drives in a run-heavy offense. Nine plays is a hint, not a trait, and the rate will come down with volume.

concerns.title: Can't win between 10 and 19 yards
concerns.body: Intermediate throws are where an NFL passer has to make a living, and he completed 26.3% of them with a -29 CPOE and two interceptions. He compensates by living short of the sticks: 5.23 intended air yards, 4.15 short of the line to gain. That keeps his yards per attempt 1.65 below the league average. With no college-to-pro track record in the dossier to suggest otherwise, treat this as a real limitation, not noise.

concerns.title: Turnovers when the game is close
concerns.body: All five interceptions came in one-score games, and close fourth quarters ran at -0.522 EPA a play with three picks. His 5.1% interception rate ranks 51st of 55. That isn't pressure-driven: his bad-throw rate is 42nd of 45. When the run game can't carry Tampa and he has to throw to win, the ball goes the wrong way.

concerns.title: Lost the starting role
concerns.body: Mayfield has started every game since Week 7. Daniels hasn't logged a meaningful snap since that 10% relief appearance at Carolina. Any value now depends on an injury ahead of him.

trend.note: He went from a turnover-marred debut against Green Bay to a clean, efficient win over a bottom-ranked Dallas defense. Then he collapsed at -18.7 EPA against Pittsburgh, and Mayfield's return sent him back to the bench.

nextGame.headline: Soft pass rush awaits, but he's holding a clipboard
nextGame.body:
On paper Carolina is a friendly opponent for this skill set. It ranks 32nd in hit rate and 31st in sack rate, which would give him time, and 21st against the pass by EPA. It does limit explosive passes (2nd), but his game isn't built on those anyway. Tampa is a 3-point favorite with a 43.5 total. Last time these teams met, the Bucs won 43-13 and Daniels got only a garbage-time series. That is the realistic ceiling here unless something happens to Mayfield.

Tampa lists no offensive injuries, so Mayfield appears set to start and Daniels' snaps depend on game script. On Carolina's side, linebacker Bobby Okereke (89% of snaps) is out. That removes the defender best suited to spying or chasing a scrambling quarterback. Top corner Jaycee Horn remains on IR, with an estimated return a week later, which thins the coverage behind a weak rush. Both would matter only if Daniels is forced into extended action.

keyMatchups.title: Clean pockets for a scrambler
keyMatchups.body: Carolina rarely gets home: 32nd in hit rate, 31st in sack rate. For a quarterback whose pressure-to-sack rate runs high, a quiet rush means fewer drive-killing sacks. If he does play, his scrambles become a choice rather than an escape.

keyMatchups.title: Coverage without Horn and Okereke
keyMatchups.body: Carolina's pass defense already ranks 21st by EPA, and it will be missing its top corner and a linebacker who plays nearly every snap. That softens exactly the underneath-to-intermediate area where Daniels struggles most.

keyMatchups.title: Blowout script brings garbage time
keyMatchups.body: Tampa is favored by 3, and the last meeting turned into a 30-point rout. That rout produced Daniels' only snaps since losing the job. A similar game is his most likely route onto the field, mostly for handoffs and scrambles.

nextGame.watch: Mayfield's health during the game: Daniels only matters if Tampa has to turn to him.

restOfSeason.body:
As long as Mayfield is healthy, expect Daniels to be a near-zero line most weeks, with an occasional late-game series in a blowout. If he's pressed into a start, the three-start sample is the best guide: about 160 to 180 passing yards, 30 to 45 rushing yards, and a turnover a game in a run-heavy plan. Tampa's 3rd-ranked defense would keep him from having to chase points.

The scramble production is the sustainable piece. The red-zone touchdown rate and the deep-ball EPA on nine attempts will regress. The intermediate struggles and close-game interceptions are the part most likely to persist, because they track with a low bad-throw ranking rather than with protection or opponents.
swingFactors: Blowout game scripts that open garbage-time series
Whether he can complete anything in the 10-19 yard range

confidence.note: Three starts, 98 attempts, no career history, and currently a backup.
